Assessing the State of Iran’s Naval Infrastructure and Tactics

Executive Summary:

The launch of the U.S.–Israeli strikes on February 28 devastated Iran’s conventional navy—the Islamic Republic of Iran Navy (IRIN)—sinking numerous frigates, corvettes, and submarines while docked or at sea.

The Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy (IRGCN) remains dangerous, despite heavy losses, due to its decentralized structure and asymmetric warfare tactics. 

The destruction proved that expensive, conventional fleets are still vulnerable to superior forces, and will likely solidify Iran’s reliance on asymmetric tactics, including land-based missiles, drones, and speedboats.

The launch of Operation Epic Fury on February 28 aimed to destroy much of Iran’s military capabilities. One day into the joint U.S.–Israeli attacks, U.S. President Donald Trump declared that Iran’s navy “will soon be floating at the bottom of the sea” (
X/@WhiteHouse, March 1).  Iranian naval infrastructure has indeed suffered crippling losses. The country appears, however, to maintain an active presence in the most sensitive parts of the Persian Gulf. It is therefore important to assess these navies’ levels of destruction and their current operational state. This major engagement, furthermore, likely portends changes for the future of both Iranian and international naval strategy. 

Two Navies, One Fate 

Iran maintains two separate naval institutions, the Islamic Republic of Iran Navy (IRIN) and the Iranian Revolutionary Guard Corps Navy (IRGCN). The IRIN  is Iran’s conventional navy and consists of large surface ships, frigates, corvettes, and submarines, used mainly for diplomacy, long-range patrols, and counter-piracy operations. The IRGCN evolved in the midst of the Iran–Iraq war (1980-88). Intended mainly for littoral operations—particularly in the Persian Gulf—the IRGCN specializes in guerrilla-style naval warfare and tactics, using fast-attack craft, short-range cruise missiles, drones, torpedoes, and mines (
Gulf International Forum, March 2026). In terms of personnel, the IRGCN is slightly larger, with 20,000 pre-war members opposed to 18,000 for the IRIN.

The IRIN has a formal command structure similar to that of other national navies and is led by Rear Admiral Shahram Irani, a Sunni Kurd. The IRGCN, on the other hand, has a decentralized command structure that seeks to foster resilience and initiative under pressure. Small IRGCN units are spread widely in concealed, hardened positions throughout the islands and inlets of the Persian Gulf, making them difficult to locate and eliminate. The entire region adjacent to the Strait of Hormuz is honeycombed with caves and hidden valleys, well-suited for concealing mobile missile systems.

Iran’s naval losses to U.S. forces during Operation Praying Mantis in April 1988 persuaded Tehran to shift to an asymmetric war model, while retaining a conventional force. After international patrols in the Gulf of Aden in 2008, Iran also began to focus on the development of a blue-water navy that would, in the words of Rear Admiral Habibollah Sayyari, deploy “from the North Pole to the South Pole,” including “warships in international waters off the [U.S.] coast … However, we will never enter the maritime borders of others, and we will not allow anybody to enter even a centimeter into our territorial waters” (
Times of Israel, September 22, 2012). In practice, IRIN ships are responsible for defensive operations in the Gulf of Oman, the Caspian Sea, and the Arabian Sea, while the IRGCN secures the Persian Gulf. 

Opening Phase Attacks 

The Israeli–American opening strikes targeted Iranian radar, communications, and naval assets at its chief port of Bandar Abbas. These were followed by strikes on the ports of Chah Bahar and Bushehr, the coastal batteries at Jask, the year-old naval base at Bandar Sirik, and the fast-attack craft base at Qeshm (
Marine Forum, March 5; 
Q News, March 31). Bandar Abbas is home to the headquarters of both the IRIN and IRGCN. The attacks diminished Iran’s integrated surveillance and maritime and air defense systems (
Gulf International Forum, March 2026). IRGC speedboat bases were also struck, destroying as much as 70 percent of their inventory (
Marine Forum, March 5). 

On March 18, the Israeli Air Force attacked the Caspian Sea port of Bandar Anzali—headquarters of the IRIN’s northern operational zone—to disrupt the shipping of Russian military supplies to Iran ( 
Ynet News, March 18; 
Militarnyi, March 19). Most of Iran’s Caspian fleet was destroyed, including a minesweeper, missile boats, the corvette 
Hamzeh
 (former personal yacht of Reza Shah, launched in 1936), and the Moudge-class frigate 
Deylaman, which sank on March 18.

Targeting Naval Leaders 

The Israeli–American campaign sought to “decapitate” Iran’s naval leadership in addition to its political leaders. On March 26, Israel claimed it had killed the head of the IRGCN, Commodore Alireza Tangsiri. He is a U.S. Specially Designated Global Terrorist (SDGT) and is believed to be responsible for leading the Iranian operations that closed the Strait of Hormuz (
Times of Israel; 
U.S. Department of Defense; 
Al-Jazeera,
  March 26). The deputy chief of IRGC naval intelligence, Behnam Rezaei, was also killed in the Israeli attack (
Iran International, March 26)

Sinking of the Moudge-Class Light Frigates 

Iranian-built ships of the Moudge-class made up the core of the regular navy’s fleet, combining air-defense systems, anti-ship cruise missiles, and anti-submarine capabilities (
Gulf International Forum, March 2026; 
Naval News, March 2). Iran identifies these ships as destroyers, but they are closer in size to light frigates or even corvettes. These ships, however,  were unable to mount a defense when attacked by U.S. warplanes.

The IRIS 
Jamaran
 was sunk at its mooring by an airstrike at Chah Bahar on March 1, while the 
Sahand
 sank after an airstrike on Bandar Abbas. The 
Sahand
 had already sunk once in an accident likely caused by a design flaw while in harbor in July 2024 before being repaired and recommissioned in November 2025 (
Business Insider,
 July 12, 2024). The IRIS 
Zagros, 
intended to be a Moudge-class frigate, was converted to a signals intelligence (SIGINT) ship after a construction accident, and was sunk by U.S. airstrikes in early March. 

The Moudge-class 1500-ton frigate 
Dena 
was
 
sunk south of Sri Lanka, 2,000 miles from Iran, on March 4. It lost up to 80 of its 180-man crew. It was struck by a torpedo from USS 
Charlotte, a Virginia-class submarine, making it only the third ship to be sunk by a torpedo since 1945. The 
Dena
 was returning to Iran from the Indian-hosted Exercise MILAN 2026 in the Bay of Bengal. The exercise included ships from 18 navies and aircraft from three others, including a U.S. P-8A Poseidon maritime patrol and reconnaissance aircraft, which may have tracked the 
Dena
 (
U.S. Navy,
 February 25; 
Military.com, March 11). 

Other Iranian ships took part in the MILAN 2026 exercise. These included the replenishment ship IRIS 
Bushehr
 and the auxiliary ship IRIS 
Lavan, 
a Hengam-class landing ship commissioned in the 1980s. Fearing further submarine attacks, the 
Bushehr
 sought refuge in Sri Lanka following the sinking of the 
Dena. After its crew of 208 was taken off in Colombo, the 
Bushehr
 was interned at Trincomalee (
Naval News, March 5). Citing technical issues, the 
Lavan
 and its 183-man crew found refuge in the Indian port of Kochi (
Deccan Herald, March 14). 

Sinking of Alvand-class Frigates and Bayandor-class Corvettes

Iran’s aging navy included four British-built frigates commissioned in the 1960s by the Imperial Iranian Navy and refitted several times since. Known as the Alvand-class, these ships were closer in size to corvettes than frigates. One of the ships from this class, the IRIS 
Sahand, was sunk by U.S. forces during the so-called Tanker War (1981–1988) when Iraq and Iran both targeted oil tankers and other merchant shipping in the Persian Gulf. 

The IRIS 
Alvand
 and the IRIS 
Sabalan
 were sunk during the February 28 attack on Bandar Abbas. The last remaining ship of the class, the 
Alborz, was in dry-dock during the attack (
Gulf International Forum, March 2026). The 
Sabalan
 had already been badly damaged in Operation Praying Mantis in 1988.

In the 1960s, the United States supplied Iran with four Texas-built corvettes, which came to be known in Iran as the Bayandor class. Two were sunk during the Iran–Iraq War of the 1980s, while the remaining two, the IRIS 
Bayandor
 and IRIS 
Naghdi,
 were destroyed in a U.S. strike on Iran’s Konarak naval base, an important outlet on the Gulf of Oman (
Naval News, March 4).

The Fate of Iran’s Submarine Fleet 

The IRIN maintains only a small number of diesel-electric attack submarines, which it struggles to keep in service. The shallow waters of the Persian Gulf present operational challenges for these larger subs. The IRIN therefore has a flotilla of 23 Ghadir-class diesel-electric mini-submarines for use in the Gulf. Patterned on a North Korean design, the mini-subs are capable of firing both torpedoes and missiles (
Nuclear Threat Initiative, September 18, 2025). 

The IRIS 
Fateh, the first of four Fateh-class submarines, was reportedly destroyed by March 3 (
Gulf News, March 4). Armed with torpedoes, mines, and cruise missiles, the 
Fateh
 was the most advanced of Iran’s underwater craft (
Naval News, February 19, 2019). The IRIS 
Taregh, a 1990s-era Russian-built Kilo-class diesel-electric submarine—one of three renamed Taregh-class subs—was sunk alongside a pier at Bandar Abbas on February 28. The other former Taregh-class submarines, the 
Nooh
 and the 
Yunes, were trapped in the harbor by damage inflicted by airstrikes, though one report suggests the 
Yunes
 may have left the harbor before the strikes (
Maritime Executive, March 1; 
Marine Forum, March 5).

Destroying the IRGC Navy 

The IRIS 
Shahid Bagheri, 
an innovative drone carrier, was one of the first U.S. targets. Operated by the IRGCN, the 
Shahid Bagheri
 was a converted South Korean container ship of 42,000 tons, refitted with a 180-meter ski-jump style flight deck and launched in November 2024. The ship carried a variety of aerial drones, helicopters, and cruise missiles and was capable of deploying guided sub-surface drones and up to 30 small high-speed patrol craft (
Naval News, February 6, 2025; 
Tasnim News Agency, February 6). The valuable ship, which had only entered service in February 2025, was disabled by U.S. airstrikes on March 2 (
Naval News, March 6; 
Gulf International Forum, March 2026).

The IRIS 
Shahid Mahdavi
 was a converted South Korean-built container ship. As a mobile base for drones, helicopters, and ballistic missiles, the ship was designed to contribute to an asymmetrical naval strategy through long-range operations. The 
Shahid Mahdavi
 sank in the Gulf of Oman after strikes by U.S. AGM-158C long-range anti-ship missiles (LRASM) (
Marine Forum, March 5).

IRGCN Shahid Soleimani-class Corvettes 

The domestically-built Shahid Soleimani-class catamaran-style corvettes were constructed with radar-reducing aluminum hulls and could reach speeds of up to 45 knots. Vertical Launch Systems (VLS) allowed the deployment of Nawab short-range, infrared-homing air defense missiles, Sayyad-3G surface-to-air missiles, and Abu Mahdi anti-ship cruise missiles. Helipads accommodated reconnaissance or attack helicopters. 

The lead ship of the class, the IRIS 
Shahid Soleimani, 
was sunk at Bandar Abbas on March 3. The next day, the IRIS
 Shahid Sayyad Shirazi 
was struck by U.S. missiles and left burning at sea. The corvette
 
was only operational for a few weeks before its destruction (
Naval News, March 4). The IRIS 
Shahid Nazeri
 was moored at Bandar Abbas when U.S. attacks began and was likely disabled or destroyed at that time (
Maritime Executive, March 1). The fate of the year-old IRIS
 Shahid Rais Ali Delvari 
was not immediately clear, but by March 11, U.S. CENTCOM claimed it had destroyed the last of the four Shahid Soleimani-class warships (
X/@CENTCOM, March 11
).  At half the size of the Shahid Soleimani-class, the catamaran missile corvette IRIS 
Abu Mahdi al-Muhandis
 did not yet have its anti-aircraft weapons installed when it was hit and sunk at Bandar Abbas on March 11 (
Janes.com, March 11).

The Forward Base Ships 

Iran’s Forward Base Ships are comparable to the U.S. Navy’s Expeditionary Mobile Base ships and are designed to handle both sea and air operations. The largest of these, the 230-meter IRIS 
Makran, was converted from a Japanese oil tanker and operated by the IRIN. The 
Makran
 was capable of supporting helicopter operations and acting as a base for operations by Special Forces groups like Iran’s Special Boat Service (SBS) (
Naval News, March 2; 
Naval News, March 11). It was last seen burning at Bandar Abbas after a March 1 U.S. airstrike (
Naval News, March 4).  

IRGCN forward base ships include the IRIS 
Shahid Roudaki, a former Italian-built cargo ship redesigned to accommodate helicopters, drones, missiles, and electronic warfare systems. The Guards also operate the undeclared forward base ship MV Saviz. It is still officially listed as a civilian merchant ship, despite being attacked with limpet mines in the Red Sea in a 2021 Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) operation. The current status of both these ships is unclear.

Iran’s Patrol Boat Strategy 

Iran’s wartime maritime strategy calls for denying access to the Persian Gulf and leveraging the complex geography of the littoral region to implement in-depth defensive measures using modern technology. A tactic favored by the IRGCN, but not yet used in the current conflict, is the swarm attack by highly maneuverable armed speed-boats, manned or unmanned. Defense against such attacks calls for eliminating as many of the boats as possible at a distance; once in close range, the multiple targets created by the “swarm” can overwhelm even modern defensive systems. In the case of speedboats armed with torpedoes or small cruise missiles, this can present a serious threat  (
Naval News, December 14, 2021).

Iran’s small boats have also taken a beating from airstrikes. Particularly, a flotilla of IRGCN 
Tondar
-class patrol boats at Bushehr naval base and IRGCN 
Zolfaghar
-class fast attack craft (patterned after a North Korean design). Some of these attacks took place at the island of Qeshm in the Strait of Hormuz, which hosts fast attack boats and missile batteries intended for use in closing the strait (
Al-Jazeera, March 17). 

Controlling Hormuz 

Iran’s defense of the Strait of Hormuz is largely land-based. Iran mainly defends the strait by aerial drones and a variety of land-based missiles and sea drones launched from hardened positions rather than using conventional naval vessels. With the addition of mines dropped from small speedboats, passage through the strait becomes a precarious enterprise, even for powerful naval vessels. Where once carriers could work their way up the Persian Gulf, today they remain distant in the safety of the Arabian Sea (
Responsible Statecraft, March 31).

Mines can have a deterrent effect greater than their operational reality. Mine-laying craft have been targeted by U.S. strikes, though estimates suggest as much as 80 percent of Iran’s mine-laying capacity survived the first two weeks of intense airstrikes (
Naval News, March 11). Any attempt to clear mines from the strait could encounter resistance from high-speed attack craft, drones, and shore-fired missiles. Intense aerial support would be necessary to find and counter such threats.

Conclusion

By April 1, U.S. authorities were claiming the destruction or disabling of over 155 Iranian warships (
U.S. Department of Defense, April 1). The utter devastation of most of the Iranian Navy in a matter of days likely confirmed Iranian naval planners’ suspicions that the highly mobile and asymmetrical approach of the IRGCN was better suited to confrontations with superior forces (
Middle East Institute, January 31, 2012). One result of the campaign has been to reduce the size and influence of the professional Iranian Navy and its leadership, with the IRGCN now ascendant.

Israel and the United States have succeeded in incapacitating Iran’s blue-water navy by aerial or submerged attacks. The IRGCN’s small craft, however, have proven more difficult to deal with. These small crafts are not so much a singular naval presence as part of an integrated defense scheme that exploits geographical advantages while deploying sensors, mobile missile systems, mines, and fast-attack craft responsive to a dispersed command-and-control structure—one capable of considerable resiliency under pressure.

The Israeli–U.S. surprise attack on February 28 allowed the partners to strike Iranian warships while still in port. The ships of the IRIN and the IRGCN were useful to the regime, if accident-prone, but it could not have escaped the attention of Iranian naval planners that the United States could sink their fleet at will. The destruction of most of Iran’s navy did not prevent Iran from closing the Strait of Hormuz; there was, in any case, no role for its conventional ships in the asymmetrical warfare being practiced successfully by the IRGC’s remaining fast-boats. One lesson that might be drawn from this conflict is the futility involved in trying to maintain an expensive naval arm that is ultimately incapable of engaging with superior forces.

Article 5 / A Member of the United Nations against which preventive or enforcement action has been taken by the Security Council may be suspended from the exercise of the rights and privileges of mem- bership by the General Assembly upon the recom- mendation of the Security Council.

Article 6 A Member of the United Nations which has persistently violated the Principles contained in the present Charter may be expelled from the Organization by the General Assembly upon the recommendation of the Security Council.

Accordingly, our respective Governments, through representatives assembled in the city of San Francisco, who have exhibited their full powers found to be in good and due form, have agreed to the present Charter of the United Nations and do hereby establish an international organization to be known as the United Nations.

related.title: Sabre-rattling to ‘tremendous love’: erratic Trump dominates final hours of Nato summit
related.summary: An erratic and at times irascible Donald Trump has said he felt a “tremendous love” from western leaders at the Nato summit, only hours after lambasting them over their defence spending and not helping the US in attacking Iran. The final summit declaration, signed off by Trump and 31 other alliance leaders, affirmed the countries’ “ironclad commitment” to article 5, which declares that an attack one Nato member is an attack on them all.
bullets: An erratic and at times irascible Donald Trump has said he felt a “tremendous love” from western leaders at the Nato summit, only hours after lambasting them over their defence spending and not helping the US in attacking Iran.

The final summit declaration, signed off by Trump and 31 other alliance leaders, affirmed the countries’ “ironclad commitment” to article 5, which declares that an attack one Nato member is an attack on them all.

Nato summits have not always taken place annually but the overwhelming concern in parts of Europe is that Trump’s grandstanding at such events risks giving hope to the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, undermining deterrence and alliance unity.

It appeared that their worst fears were being realised when Trump appeared on Wednesday morning with the Nato secretary general, Mark Rutte, and began with a lengthy monologue airing a string of grievances with Nato and several individual members, as well as attacking the leadership of Iran.

Trump said he was “very upset with Nato” and complained that alliance members “didn’t want to help us with the number one state sponsor of terror, that’s Iran”, a reference a refusal by European countries apart from the UK to allow the US to publicly carry out bombing missions from Europe’s airbases.
related.excerpt: An erratic and at times irascible Donald Trump has said he felt a “tremendous love” from western leaders at the Nato summit, only hours after lambasting them over their defence spending and not helping the US in attacking Iran. The US president’s mixed messaging dominated the final hours of the two-day gathering in Ankara, Turkey, beginning with him publicly calling Iran’s leadership scum and renewing his demand for control of Greenland. He then adopted a softer tone in a private meeting of 32 Nato leaders in the late morning, where he did not mention Greenland or other earlier criticisms, and instead told allies that “we want to remain with you”. “It was a great meeting, there was a lot of love in that room, a lot of unity,” Trump said soon after at a bilateral meeting with Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, which included a surprise offer to licence the manufacturing of Patriot air defence missiles to Ukraine. Trump concluded by hosting a rambling press conference that barely addressed Nato topics, but where he praised Turkey’s strongman president, Recep Tayyip Erdoğan, talked up the US economy and said he was “No 1 on TikTok”.
